function.arguments: {"accession": "A0A0F7RJ52", "reason": "AsbA (spermidine-citrate ligase, Bacillus anthracis; reviewed, protein-level evidence) natively ligates a free carboxylic acid to a free primary amine through an ATP/acyl-adenylate route. Activity with cadaverine is not shown.", "mechanism_and_step": "Citrate carboxylate attacks the ATP alpha-phosphate to give citryl-AMP and PPi. A spermidine terminal primary amine (N8) then attacks the acyl-AMP carbonyl, forming an amide and releasing AMP. In the target, one glutarate carboxylate would be adenylated and one cadaverine NH2 would attack it. The step is the adenylate aminolysis.", "revisit_when": "Revisit if a primary source or assay shows AsbA activity on a simple linear dicarboxylate such as glutarate or adipate, or on cadaverine or putrescine. Docking or structural comparison of glutarate in the citrate site would also help. function.description: Record one source-grounded target relevance assessment.

function.name: record_target_assessment
function.arguments: {"accession": "A0A0F7RJ52", "reason": "AsbA (Spermidine-citrate ligase, NIS synthetase) is the only candidate with recorded tolerance on both sides: free-small-molecule amide ligation with diamine analogs and a citrate analog. The acid partner is the limiting uncertainty. The record contains no glutarate data.", "mechanism_and_step": "ATP-dependent adenylation of a citrate carboxylate gives acyl-AMP and PPi. The terminal primary amine of spermidine then attacks the acyl-AMP to form the amide. For the target, one glutarate carboxylate would be adenylated, and one cadaverine NH2 would attack it. Mono-amide formation is the expected first step.", "revisit_when": "Raise priority if glutarate or other dicarboxylates show ATP-dependent turnover with AsbA or a close NIS homolog, or if docking of glutarate-AMP near the diamine site gives a catalytically compatible geometry. Lower it if only tricarboxylic acids are accepted.", "decision": "investigate", "evidence_level": "mechanistic_transfer", "target_roles": [{"participant": "T1", "role": "Acyl donor. One carboxylate is adenylated by ATP. Native counterpart is citrate (native:0:0), the adenylated carboxymethyl carboxylate.", "basis": "transfer"}, {"participant": "T2", "role": "Amine nucleophile. One terminal NH2 attacks acyl-AMP. Native counterpart is the terminal primary amine of spermidine (native:1:0).", "basis": "transfer"}], "strengths": ["Reviewed entry with experimental native activity (PubMed 17579415, 19259597, 22408253) for free-small-molecule amide formation via acyl-AMP.", "Function comment states AsbA condenses several di- and triamine analogs of spermidine with citrate, which supports T2 binding as a linear polyamine-like acceptor.", "Function comment states AsbA condenses tricarballylic acid (citrate analog lacking the hydroxyl) with spermidine, so the acyl donor tolerates some change."], "unknowns": ["Whether cadaverine itself is among the accepted diamine analogs; the record does not name them.", "Whether the citrate-binding site accepts a dicarboxylate lacking the central carboxyl and hydroxyl.", "Relative activity versus native turnover; the comment records condensation but not rates.", "Whether mono-amide release or further polymerization occurs."], "constraints": [{"finding": "Glutarate (132 Da, linear dicarboxylate, no hydroxyl or third carboxylate) differs from citrate (tricarboxylate with hydroxyl). The record has no dicarboxylate or glutarate evidence for T1, the limiting partner.", "basis": "missing_evidence", "severity": "major"}, {"finding": "Cadaverine is shorter than spermidine and has no secondary amine.", "basis": "observed_mismatch", "severity": "minor"}], "source_refs": ["R1"]}

function.arguments: {"accession": "A0A0S2IKQ5", "reason": "Populus asparagine synthetase (glutamine-hydrolyzing) forms aspartyl-AMP, but its acyl donor is an α-amino acid and its nucleophile is ammonia delivered from glutamine. Neither target partner has a defensible match. The entry is an unreviewed, automatically inferred annotation.", "mechanism_and_step": "The C-terminal synthetase domain adenylates the aspartate β-carboxylate with ATP (acyl-AMP plus PPi). Cadaverine as a direct nucleophile would need a bulky amine to reach the acyl-AMP site.", "revisit_when": "Reopen if this or a close asparagine synthetase shows ATP-dependent amide formation with a bulky primary amine or a non-α-amino dicarboxylate. The native nucleophile is NH3 released from glutamine (native:1:0), which acts as the ammonia carrier and is not the direct nucleophile.", "basis": "hypothesis"}], "strengths": [], "unknowns": ["Whether the synthetase pocket accepts a carboxylate lacking the α-amino and α-carboxyl motif.", "Whether any non-ammonia amine can reach the acyl-AMP, either via the ammonia tunnel or from solution.", "Measured activity of this exact Populus protein; the annotation is automatically inferred (ARBA and PIRNR)."], "constraints": [{"finding": "The native nucleophile is NH3 channelled from the glutamine domain. Cadaverine is a much larger linear diamine, so T2 has no matched native partner.", "basis": "missing_evidence", "severity": "major"}, {"finding": "The native acyl donor is an α-amino acid. No evidence shows turnover of glutarate, which lacks the α-amine.", "basis": "missing_evidence", "severity": "major"}, {"finding": "The record is unreviewed (TrEMBL) with transcript-level evidence and an automatically inferred reaction.", "basis": "missing_evidence", "severity": "minor"}], "source_refs": ["R2"]}

function.arguments: {"accession": "A0A0F7RJ52", "reason": "Spermidine-citrate ligase (AsbA, B. anthracis) is a reviewed NIS synthetase with experimentally cited native activity. Its cited function text reports condensation of several di- and triamine spermidine analogs with citrate, and of tricarballylic acid (citrate without the hydroxyl) with spermidine. That is relevant promiscuity at both target partners. This is the only candidate with such evidence. I have not read the primary papers for kinetics or relative rates, so detectable versus efficient turnover is unresolved.", "mechanism_and_step": "ATP-dependent adenylation of a citrate carboxyl, releasing PPi, gives an acyl-AMP. A primary amine of spermidine then attacks it to form an amide with AMP leaving. For the target, one glutarate carboxylate would be adenylated (T1). One terminal NH2 of cadaverine would be the nucleophile (T2). The ATP and Mg2+ requirement matches the target's implied cofactor needs.", "revisit_when": "Revisit if the primary studies (PMID 19259597, 17579415) show that the diamine and tricarballylate analogs turn over poorly or only at a bound-adenylate stage. Priority rises if a glutarate or cadaverine assay, or a co-fold, shows the carboxylate reaching the activated-carbon position.", "decision": "prioritize", "evidence_level": "mechanistic_transfer", "target_roles": [{"participant": "T1", "role": "Acyl donor. One carboxylate is adenylated in place of a citrate carboxylate (native occurrence native:0:0, citrate, stoichiometry 1).", "basis": "transfer"}, {"participant": "T2", "role": "Amine nucleophile. function.arguments: {"accession": "A0A1H2LYA1", "reason": "This D-Ala-D-Ala ligase (ATP-grasp) is an automatically inferred, unreviewed entry. function.name: record_target_assessment
function.description: Record one source-grounded target relevance assessment.

accession.description: Exact supplied accession only. Put the protein name in reason, never in accession.

source_refs.description: Only this candidate's supplied R-indexed source ID. Describe paper citations in the rationale; do not add them here.

function.name: record_target_assessment
function.arguments: {"accession": "A0A5J9TLB9", "reason": "Asparagine synthetase (glutamine-hydrolyzing, Eragrostis curvula). The record is unreviewed TrEMBL with only automatic annotation (ARBA/PIRNR) and predicted existence. It has real acyl-adenylate chemistry, but the cadaverine partner has no supported role.", "mechanism_and_step": "Native chemistry: the Asp side-chain carboxylate attacks ATP Palpha to give β-aspartyl-AMP plus PPi. NH3 released by the glutaminase domain from Gln is channelled to this intermediate. Target hypothesis: glutarate carboxylate becomes glutaryl-AMP, then cadaverine N attacks the acyl carbon. Step: amine attack on acyl-AMP. This needs an external amine to reach the synthetase site, which is normally supplied only by an internal ammonia tunnel.", "revisit_when": "Evidence shows this or a close homolog turns over a non-ammonia amine or a non-α-amino diacid, or an ammonia-independent synthetase activity is shown to accept alkylamines.", "decision": "defer", "evidence_level": "speculative", "target_roles": [{"participant": "T1", "role": "Acyl donor to ATP, analogous to the Asp β-carboxylate (native:0:0). Glutarate has no α-amino group and is one carbon longer.", "basis": "transfer"}, {"participant": "T2", "role": "Nucleophile in place of tunnelled NH3. Native Gln (native:1:0) is only the ammonia donor and is not the direct nucleophile, so it has no target counterpart.", "basis": "hypothesis"}], "strengths": ["Acyl-adenylate (ATP to AMP+PPi) chemistry on a free small-molecule dicarboxylate matches the target activation route."], "unknowns": ["Whether the synthetase site binds a diacid without an α-amino group.", "Whether cadaverine can reach the acyl-AMP, since the native nucleophile is NH3 delivered through a tunnel.", "Native activity here is inferred only."], "constraints": [{"finding": "Native nucleophile is ammonia from an internal channel (MW 17), versus cadaverine (MW 102). This is a major size/access mismatch.", "basis": "observed_mismatch", "severity": "major"}, {"finding": "No evidence of acceptance of glutarate or any alkylamine; recognition of the Asp α-amino/α-carboxylate is untested for glutarate.", "basis": "missing_evidence", "severity": "major"}], "source_refs": ["R1"]}

function.arguments: {"accession": "Q81RQ8", "reason": "Citryl-spermidine/3,4-dihydroxybenzoyl-citryl-spermidine:spermidine ligase (AsbB, Bacillus anthracis). function.arguments: {"accession": "A0A5J9TLB9", "reason": "Asparagine synthetase (Eragrostis curvula) has ATP-dependent acyl-AMP chemistry, but both target partners differ from native roles. The target would need glutarate activated to glutaryl-AMP and cadaverine to reach the synthetase site in place of channeled NH3.", "revisit_when": "Direct evidence shows this or a close ASNS orthologue accepting an exogenous alkylamine or a non-amino dicarboxylate, or a structure shows the synthetase site is accessible to a C5 diamine without the Gln-derived ammonia tunnel.", "decision": "defer", "evidence_level": "speculative", "target_roles": [{"participant": "T1", "role": "Would replace L-Asp (native:0:0) as the acyl donor, with one carboxylate activated as acyl-AMP. Glutarate has no alpha-amino group and a longer chain.", "basis": "hypothesis"}, {"participant": "T2", "role": "Would replace NH3 liberated from L-Gln (native:1:0) as the nucleophile. Gln is only the ammonia carrier and has no target counterpart. Water is a native co-substrate that is not a target partner.", "basis": "hypothesis"}], "strengths": ["Native acyl-AMP chemistry makes a C-N amide bond from a carboxylate with ATP, ending in AMP + PPi.", "Asp is a C4 dicarboxylate, similar in size to glutarate (same MW 132.1)."], "unknowns": ["Whether the synthetase site binds a carboxylate lacking the alpha-amino group.", "Whether the synthetase site can bind cadaverine directly, or whether its ammonia-delivery route admits only NH3.", "Whether the native Gln-dependent step is required for turnover."], "constraints": [{"finding": "The native nucleophile is NH3 (about 18 Da), channeled intramolecularly from Gln. D-alanine is then activated by the NRPS uncD that transfers it to the PKS uncA to produce R-dihydroxymethyl isoindolinone. UncG then produces the tetrapeptide L-Leu-D-Isd-L-Ala-L-Gln by adding L-Ala-L-Gln produced by the dipeptide synthetase uncJ that forms L-Ala-L-Gln from L-Ala and L-Gln. function.arguments: {"accession": "A0A023X242", "reason": "Unreviewed TrEMBL entry (Protein involved in propanediol utilization and related proteins, Rubrobacter radiotolerans) with predicted-only existence, no catalytic activity and no function comment. Its only support is a GHMP kinase domain architecture (N-terminal IPR006204, C-terminal IPR013750). That does not give a defensible amide-ligation hypothesis.", "mechanism_and_step": "GHMP kinases typically phosphorylate hydroxyl groups with ATP. function.arguments: {"accession": "P0AES0", "reason": "Bifunctional glutathionylspermidine synthetase/amidase (E. coli K12). Swiss-Prot with experimentally cited synthetase and amidase activity. function.arguments: {"accession": "A0A023X242", "reason": "Rubrobacter radiotolerans PduX-like protein (GHMP kinase N/C-terminal domains) has no recorded catalytic activity and is TrEMBL \"Predicted\" (existence level 4). Nothing in the record supports carboxyl activation or amide-bond formation.", "mechanism_and_step": "GHMP kinases typically phosphorylate a hydroxyl with ATP. Here no native substrate, no acyl-phosphate or acyl-adenylate chemistry, and no amine acceptor is annotated. No target step (carboxyl activation or aminolysis) can be assigned.", "revisit_when": "Experimental evidence shows this exact protein uses a carboxylate as an ATP-dependent phosphoryl acceptor, or turns over a free amine in an acyl-transfer step.", "decision": "defer", "evidence_level": "speculative", "target_roles": [{"participant": "T1", "role": "Would need to be the activated acyl donor; no carboxylate-activating site is annotated.", "basis": "hypothesis"}, {"participant": "T2", "role": "Would need to be the amine nucleophile; no amine-accepting step is annotated.", "basis": "hypothesis"}], "strengths": [], "unknowns": ["Native reaction and substrate are unknown", "Whether the kinase fold can phosphorylate a carboxylate", "Whether any amine can attack the product"], "constraints": [{"finding": "No catalytic-activity annotation; bond type, direction and native reaction claims are all insufficient_evidence.", "basis": "missing_evidence", "severity": "major"}, {"finding": "No acyl-activation chemistry is evident from the record (GHMP kinase domains only).", "basis": "missing_evidence", "severity": "major"}], "source_refs": ["R1"]}

function.arguments: {"accession": "A0A060LXV4", "reason": "PduX-type protein from Shouchella lehensis is classed as an L-threonine kinase (IPR012363) and is TrEMBL \"Predicted\" with no recorded reaction. The family implies phosphorylation of a hydroxyl, not carboxyl activation.", "mechanism_and_step": "The likely native step is ATP-dependent O-phosphorylation of an L-threonine hydroxyl. The target needs carboxylate activation followed by amine attack, and nothing links this protein to either step.", "revisit_when": "Experimental data show this exact protein phosphorylates or adenylylates a carboxylate, or catalyzes any acyl transfer to a primary amine.", "decision": "defer", "evidence_level": "speculative", "target_roles": [{"participant": "T1", "role": "Would need to be the activated acyl donor; the family phosphorylates a hydroxyl of an amino acid.", "basis": "hypothesis"}, {"participant": "T2", "role": "Would need to be the amine nucleophile; no amine-acceptor step is known.", "basis": "hypothesis"}], "strengths": [], "unknowns": ["Experimental activity of this exact protein", "Whether a threonine-binding pocket tolerates a dicarboxylate or a diamine", "Any amide-forming step"], "constraints": [{"finding": "No catalytic-activity annotation; the family-level threonine kinase assignment is not an amide-forming activity.", "basis": "missing_evidence", "severity": "major"}, {"finding": "Native-substrate recognition is tied to an alpha-amino acid (threonine).", "basis": "missing_evidence", "severity": "minor"}], "source_refs": ["R2"]}

function.arguments: {"accession": "A0A0B4EYZ4", "reason": "Metarhizium epsilon-poly-L-lysine synthase has an adenylation-type (AMP-binding) domain, an ACP/phosphopantetheine domain and a Pls/PosA C-terminal region. Cadaverine resembles the lysine side chain, but the donor site is expected to be tuned to an alpha-amino acid.", "revisit_when": "There is experimental evidence that the adenylation domain activates a non-alpha-amino dicarboxylic acid, or that the enzyme acylates a free diamine without a lysine backbone.", "decision": "defer", "evidence_level": "speculative", "target_roles": [{"participant": "T1", "role": "Hypothetical acyl donor adenylated at the A domain. It lacks the lysine alpha-carboxylate and alpha-amine.", "basis": "hypothesis"}], "strengths": [], "unknowns": ["Experimental activity and substrate scope of this exact protein", "Whether the A domain accepts a non-amino diacid", "Whether free-molecule turnover occurs without carrier-bound donors"], "constraints": [{"finding": "No native-reaction annotation; ACP/carrier-protein architecture suggests carrier-tethered intermediates.", "basis": "missing_evidence", "severity": "major"}, {"finding": "Both partners would need a lysine-like alpha-amino acid recognition motif that glutarate and cadaverine lack.", "basis": "missing_evidence", "severity": "major"}], "source_refs": ["R3"]}

function.name: record_target_assessment
function.arguments: {"accession": "C4JF81", "reason": "uncJ (ATP-grasp enzyme) is a reviewed dipeptide synthetase with experimentally cited L-Ala + L-Gln + ATP → L-Ala-L-Gln + ADP + Pi (PubMed 40387549). The mechanism is a true acyl-phosphate amide ligase, but both native partners are alpha-amino acids.", "mechanism_and_step": "The ATP gamma-phosphate forms an acyl-phosphate on the L-Ala carboxylate (native:0:0), and the L-Gln alpha-amine (native:1:0) attacks it. Glutarate would map to the Ala donor and cadaverine to the Gln nucleophile. function.name: record_target_assessment
function.arguments: {"accession": "A0A0B4EYZ4", "reason": "Metarhizium anisopliae epsilon-poly-L-lysine synthase (A0A0B4EYZ4) is unreviewed with predicted existence and no recorded reaction. It has an AMP-binding (ANL) adenylation domain, an ACP/phosphopantetheine domain and a Pls/PosA C-terminal region. The adenylation domain gives acyl-adenylate chemistry. The Pls-type name suggests iterative amide formation onto an aminoalkyl lysine side-chain amine, which loosely resembles cadaverine's aminopentyl end and a polyamide product. This is a name-based inference only. The enzyme's presumed native donor is an alpha-amino acid, and the carrier-protein domain adds a tethering concern.", "mechanism_and_step": "Acyl-adenylate route (ATP to AMP + PPi). Glutarate carboxylate would be adenylated, then possibly thioesterified on the ACP domain, then attacked by cadaverine N1. Native partner roles are inferred from the protein name, not recorded: an L-lysine carboxylate as acyl donor and a lysine epsilon-amine as nucleophile.", "revisit_when": "Revisit if the adenylation domain is shown to adenylate non-alpha-amino acids or dicarboxylates, or if free-amine acceptors other than lysine are accepted without a carrier-bound donor.", "decision": "investigate", "evidence_level": "mechanistic_transfer", "target_roles": [{"participant": "T1", "role": "Acyl donor adenylated by the ANL domain. Presumed native counterpart is the L-lysine carboxylate, which also has an alpha-amine that glutarate lacks (unverified).", "basis": "transfer"}, {"participant": "T2", "role": "Amine nucleophile. Presumed native counterpart is the lysine epsilon-amine on a chain. Cadaverine's aminopentyl end is similar, but its distal charged amine is a difference.", "basis": "hypothesis"}], "strengths": ["AMP-binding ANL adenylation domain (IPR000873, conserved AMP-binding site IPR020845) provides acyl-adenylate chemistry", "Pls/PosA C-terminal domain (IPR012728) points to polyamide-forming architecture, which is relevant to the polymeric target"], "unknowns": ["Adenylation domain substrate specificity", "Whether a free small acyl donor is turned over or activity depends on the carrier domain", "Whether the C-terminal region accepts an aliphatic diamine"], "constraints": [{"finding": "Native donor is presumably an alpha-amino acid; glutarate has no alpha-amine and a distal carboxylate, so the limiting T1 recognition is unsupported.", "basis": "missing_evidence", "severity": "major"}, {"finding": "No catalytic activity is recorded for this protein, and the ACP domain suggests carrier-protein dependence with unproven free-molecule turnover.", "basis": "missing_evidence", "severity": "major"}], "source_refs": ["R3"]}

function.arguments: {"accession": "C4JF81", "reason": "Uncinocarpus reesii ATP-grasp dipeptide synthetase uncJ (C4JF81) is reviewed, with experimentally cited L-Ala-L-Gln formation (PubMed 40387549). Glutarate also has a second distal carboxylate that the native donor does not.", "basis": "hypothesis"}, {"participant": "T2", "role": "Amine nucleophile. Presumed native counterpart is the L-Gln alpha-amine, which also carries an alpha-carboxylate and a side-chain amide. function.arguments: {"accession": "C7P8V7", "reason": "Methanocaldococcus fervens tyramine--L-glutamate ligase MfnD (C7P8V7) is reviewed, with experimentally cited activity (PubMed 25211225). It is an ATP-grasp enzyme that forms an amide between a free amine and the gamma-carboxylate of L-glutamate. It also accepts phenylethylamine in vitro, which is relevant amine promiscuity. This is the closest role match among the candidates. The limiting partner is cadaverine, because no aliphatic or diamine acceptor has been shown. Rates for non-native substrates are not reported in the record.", "mechanism_and_step": "ATP-grasp acyl-phosphate route (ATP to ADP + Pi). Native:0:0 (L-glutamate, stoichiometry 1) is the donor, activated at the gamma-carboxylate. Native:1:0 (tyramine, stoichiometry 1) is the amine nucleophile. Glutarate would be activated at one carboxylate, with its other carboxylate standing in for glutamate's alpha-carboxylate. Cadaverine N1 would attack the acyl phosphate.", "revisit_when": "Revisit if measured data show turnover of glutarate or of an aliphatic or distal-amine acceptor. Reprioritize if aliphatic amines are accepted.", "decision": "investigate", "evidence_level": "mechanistic_transfer", "target_roles": [{"participant": "T1", "role": "Acyl donor, with one carboxylate activated. Native counterpart is the L-glutamate gamma-carboxylate. Glutarate matches the C5 diacid backbone but lacks the alpha-ammonium. The two carboxylates are symmetric.", "basis": "transfer"}, {"participant": "T2", "role": "Amine nucleophile. Native counterpart is tyramine's primary amine.
